title: Medical Necessity in Coding and Billing

sections.learningObjectives:
- Define medical necessity and explain the elements of services that are reasonable and necessary for diagnosis or treatment.
- Relate clinical documentation, including diagnosis-to-procedure linkage, to establishing medical necessity.
- Recognize coverage determination concepts, including National and Local Coverage Determinations, prior authorization, and Advance Beneficiary Notices.
- Apply scope-of-practice boundaries by gathering and routing information and escalating medical necessity determinations to clinicians and billing professionals.
- Identify documentation and coding practices that prevent medical necessity denials and avoid fraud and abuse.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Medical necessity is like a doctor only ordering the medicine that actually matches your sickness, not whatever you ask for at the counter.

### Question 2

The rulebook says a test or treatment has to actually be needed to figure out or fix a health problem, not just be something nice to have.

### Question 3

If you get a snack just because you want one and not because you are hungry, that snack is for convenience. Medical care works the same way: it has to be needed.

### Question 4

A treatment is necessary when it matches the problem the patient actually has, the way the right key matches the right lock.

### Question 5

You do not use a fire hose to water one houseplant; you use just the right amount. Medical care should use just the right amount too.

### Question 6

A raincoat is a reasonable thing to own, but it is not necessary on a sunny day. Both parts have to be true for care to be covered.

### Question 7

Each item on a shopping list is checked against the recipe separately; each service on a claim is checked for necessity on its own.

### Question 8

Whether a bandage is needed depends on whether you have a cut, not on whether you prefer the blue box over the red box.

### Question 9

Before a store will pay for a repair under warranty, the repair has to be needed. Medicare works the same way: it only pays for care that is actually needed.

### Question 10

Being on the menu does not mean the dish is right for your diet; a covered service still has to be the right one for the patient's health problem.

### Question 11

A brand-new medicine still being tested in a lab is not yet a proven treatment, so insurance usually waits until it is proven to work safely.

### Question 12

It is like a teacher checking that each answer on a test is actually correct before giving points, so points only go to real, correct work.

### Question 13

The medical record is like a receipt that shows exactly what was done and why it was needed.

### Question 14

If there is no note about a test in the chart, it is like there is no proof the test was ever needed, even if it happened.

### Question 15

The diagnosis code is the label for the health problem; the label is what tells the insurance why the service was needed.

### Question 16

Sending in a bill with no explanation of why the work was needed is like asking to be paid without showing what the job was for.

### Question 17

The diagnosis and the procedure must fit together like a puzzle: the diagnosis is the reason, and the procedure is what was done about it.

### Question 18

The chart note is the story of the visit: what the patient told the doctor, what the doctor found, and why the doctor chose that treatment.

### Question 19

If two puzzle pieces do not fit, you ask the person who made the puzzle rather than forcing them together.

### Question 20

The doctor decides what care is needed, and the insurance company checks whether it will pay; the assistant helps by moving the information between them.

### Question 21

Charging for a large pizza when only a small one was made is upcoding; the bill must match what was actually done.

### Question 22

If a homework answer is missing, you ask the teacher to explain it instead of writing in a made-up answer.

### Question 23

A note that is real, readable, and signed by the doctor is like a receipt that proves who did the work and when.

### Question 24

Copying yesterday's note into today's chart is like copying last week's homework and pretending it is today's; the answers may no longer fit.

### Question 25

The Assessment and Plan is the part where the doctor writes down the problem and the plan to fix it, which is exactly why the tests and treatments are needed.

### Question 26

If the reason for the test is not written down, the insurance has no way to know the test was needed, so it may say no.

### Question 27

You need a doctor's note that says why a wheelchair or walker is actually needed, not just a wish for one.

### Question 28

It is matching the reason (diagnosis) to the action (procedure) so the bill makes sense.

### Question 29

An NCD is like a national rulebook page that says whether Medicare will pay for a certain kind of care anywhere in the country.

### Question 30

An LCD is like a local rule for one region, made by the office that handles Medicare claims for that area.

### Question 31

The regional Medicare claims office writes the local coverage rules, not the people inside one doctor's office.

### Question 32

An NCD is a country-wide rule; an LCD is a regional rule. Big rule versus local rule.

### Question 33

It is like checking the rules of a game before you make a move, so you do not lose points for a move that is not allowed.

### Question 34

The plan covers the medicine in general, but it does not fit this patient's problem, so the plan says no for this patient.

### Question 35

Being allowed in the store (covered) is different from having the right coupon for your purchase (necessary for you).

### Question 36

Prior authorization is like getting a permission slip before the field trip, not after you have already gone.

### Question 37

An ABN is like a heads-up note: "This might not be paid for; do you still want it?" so the patient can choose.

### Question 38

If a judge says no, you look at why and gather your evidence before you appeal, rather than filing the same paper again.

### Question 39

To win an appeal, you show your proof: the doctor's notes that explain why the care was needed.

### Question 40

It is a guardrail that catches a bill charging for 10 of something when only 1 or 2 would ever be needed at once.

### Question 41

Fixing a nose so a person can breathe is necessary; changing a nose just for looks is not something insurance usually pays for.

### Question 42

The plan pays for one checkup a year; if you ask for five, the plan pays for the one it thinks is needed and not the extras.

### Question 43

The assistant is the messenger who checks the rules and shares the answer, not the referee who makes the final call.

### Question 44

Coverage is whether the service is on the approved list; necessity is whether the service is right for this patient's problem. You need both.

### Question 45

If the rule says only certain health problems qualify, and this patient's problem is not on the list, you tell the team instead of changing the answer to fit.

### Question 46

An audit is a careful re-check of the patient's chart to make sure the bill matches what really happened and was really needed.

### Question 47

If a patient has both a sprained ankle and a cold, the ankle is the reason for the ankle X-ray, not the cold.

### Question 48

If the reason for a picture is not written down, you ask the doctor to write it down, rather than making up a reason yourself.

### Question 49

It is like laws from the whole country, then rules for the state, then rules for your town, then the decision on your own case.

### Question 50

The ABN is a signed heads-up that lets the office send the bill to the patient if the insurance says no.

### Question 51

If you do not warn the patient first with a signed note, you may not be allowed to hand them the bill later.

### Question 52

Some things are simply not on the list of what Medicare will ever pay for, no matter how much they might be needed.

### Question 53

A checkup when you feel fine and a test because you feel sick are different situations, so the rules about paying for them are different too.

### Question 54

The level of a visit is set by how much thinking and checking the patient's problem actually needed, all written in the note.

### Question 55

A modifier is like a note in the margin explaining a special situation, not a magic word that forces approval.

### Question 56

The -25 flag is only used when the doctor truly did a separate extra piece of work on top of the procedure, and the note shows it.

### Question 57

When someone asks for specific proof, you send exactly the right papers, not the whole filing cabinet, and you never change them.

### Question 58

If you see someone fudging the numbers, you tell the teacher or the referee, not the other players.

### Question 59

You can never write down something that did not really happen just to get a bill paid; that is cheating.

### Question 60

Lying on an important form to get money can get a person in big trouble with the law.

### Question 61

The honest answer is: "Let me check the rules for you," not a made-up yes or no.

### Question 62

What matters is how sick or injured the patient was on the day of care, written down at that time.

### Question 63

You get the right level of care in the right place, like using a bandage at home instead of staying overnight in a hospital for a paper cut.

### Question 64

If a splinter can be removed at home, going to the emergency room for it is more than what is needed.

### Question 65

If the treatment does not match the problem, insurance has a reason to say it was not needed.

### Question 66

Almost everything a doctor orders, from a test to a bandage to a treatment, has to be needed for the patient's problem.

### Question 67

The care should match what trained doctors generally agree is the right way to treat that problem.

### Question 68

Reasonable means the amount and kind of care make sense for the problem, not that it is the cheapest or fastest.

### Question 69

Making sure the label on the bill truly matches what was wrong and what was done keeps the bill from being rejected.

### Question 70

The code must come from what is actually written in the chart, not from guesses or wishes.

### Question 71

Coding is turning the doctor's written notes into the right number codes, not inventing codes to make more money.

### Question 72

When something goes wrong with a bill, the assistant explains what happened and what can be done, calmly and kindly.

### Question 73

Medical decision-making is how much careful thinking the patient's problem required from the doctor.

### Question 74

If the receipt shows two items but the bill charges for four, the store fixes the bill to match the receipt.

### Question 75

Write down why the test is being done when the doctor orders it, so the reason is clear from the start.

### Question 76

The insurance company's reviewers check the chart to decide whether the care met the rules for being paid.

### Question 77

A right note with the wrong label can still cause the bill to be turned away, because the label must match the note.

### Question 78

The note should say why the patient is being sent to a specialist or why an extra test is needed.

### Question 79

First write down the problem and the need, then attach the right label, then send the bill; the insurance checks each step.

### Question 80

The LCD is the rule about what is covered; the article is the how-to instructions for coding and billing that rule.

### Question 81

When in doubt, ask the person who knows and check the rulebook before sending the bill.

### Question 82

Something can be genuinely needed but still not be on the list of what this particular plan pays for; then the cost may fall to the patient.

### Question 83

The chart note is the proof that the care was really needed, like a receipt that proves what was bought.

### Question 84

The assistant is the helper who gathers the papers and passes them to the right person, not the one who makes the final medical call.

### Question 85

If the rule says the test needs one of a few listed reasons, first check whether one is truly there and ask the doctor to document it; if not, the denial may be final.
